articleSummary: New World screwworm fly (Cochliomyia hominivorax) resurgence in Mexico has infected more than 500 people. A study of 202 confirmed myiasis cases from April 2025–March 2026 shows rising incidence: 2025 averaged ~3 weekly cases, 2026 over 9. Six deaths occurred; one directly due to infestation, others with comorbidities such as cancer, encephalitis, respiratory failure, or septic shock. The cohort was 72% male, ages 12–93 (mean 61); ~77% had preexisting conditions (diabetes, alcoholism, cancer, dermatologic disease). Legs and feet accounted for 55% of infections; head/neck regions—including nose, mouth, and eyes—were also affected. Eggs laid on wounds hatch in ~24 hours; larvae consume living tissue and can invade muscle, bone, or skull without prompt treatment. Cross-sector prevention—surveillance, health-care training, animal-transport controls, and integrated actions across human, animal, wildlife, and agriculture sectors—are essential. US reported 45 animal cases; no human transmission; CDC estimates ~2,360 human infections in Central America; in Brazil, a March 2026 fatality in Ribeirão Preto highlights vulnerability.

articleSummary: Two frontline vaccinators, Shameema and Tanzeela in Pulwama, Indian-administered Kashmir, trek daily to reach Gujjar and Bakarwal nomadic families, delivering oral polio vaccine to children under five. articleSummary: Hantavirus in Jambi Province, Indonesia: Residents urged to beware of symptoms, sources and spread. Rodents such as rats and mice carry hantavirus, which can cause severe kidney and lung disease. The virus is shed in rodent droppings, urine, and saliva; main human transmission occurs when contaminated dust is inhaled or via bites. Dry-cleaning of rodent-infested spaces—especially warehouses or old buildings—can aerosolize particles, so dry sweeping is strongly discouraged. Human-to-human transmission is considered very rare. The term hantavirus originated after the Hantan River in Korea, though awareness has existed long before. At-risk groups include workers cleaning old warehouses, farmers in plantations, and construction workers in aging structures. Prevention emphasizes preventing rodent access and applying PHBS (Clean and Healthy Living Habits).

articleSummary: A 10-year-old developed plantar warts after swimming, diagnosed as infection with human papillomavirus (HPV). HPV comprises over 200 types; cutaneous HPV strains cause plantar warts and other skin lesions, not linked to sexual transmission or cervical cancer high-risk types. Incubation is 2–6 months, so infection may not originate from that session. Transmission occurs via direct skin contact or shared items; public showers, towels, footwear, and pool edges can spread the virus, especially through damaged skin. Chinese pool standards (GB 37488-2019) require residual chlorine 0.3–1.0 mg/L, pH 7.0–7.8, turbidity ≤1 NTU, total bacterial count ≤200 CFU/mL, and no E. coli; chlorine inactivates pathogens over time, and Cryptosporidium can survive >7 days even in compliant water. Prevention: choose well-managed venues, shower before entering water, wear slippers, bring personal towels, avoid swallowing pool water, and avoid swimming with diarrhea or open wounds.

articleHeadline: Case Study: Rare Recurrence of AAV in Kidney Transplant Recipient With Tuberculosis
articleSummary: A 28-year-old man from Brazil with end-stage renal disease due to granulomatosis with polyangiitis received a kidney transplant in 2019 from his mother. One year before transplantation he had a positive C-ANCA (1:40). In 2025 he was treated for active pulmonary tuberculosis (RIPE regimen), during which rifampicin lowered tacrolimus levels, prompting dose adjustments in his triple immunosuppressive therapy (tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, prednisone). Post-transplant, he developed fever, allograft dysfunction, proteinuria, hematuria, and rising C-ANCA; renal biopsy showed pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis consistent with recurrent ANCA-associated vasculitis. Immunosuppression was intensified with cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids, then rituximab, leading to improved renal function without infectious deterioration as TB treatment concluded. Authors highlight that infection or its treatment can paradoxically trigger AAV reactivation in transplant recipients and stress close immunosuppression monitoring, individualized management, and multidisciplinary decision-making to balance infection control with autoimmunity treatment.

articleSummary: As of 11 August 2026, dengue management in Brazil advises extreme caution with dental care during the acute phase. If platelet count falls below 50,000/mm3, invasive dental procedures (extractions, implants, gum surgery) risk severe bleeding and hypovolemic shock, so elective/invasive work is prohibited until 48 hours after fever ends. Noninvasive assessments and oral hygiene guidance are allowed. Oral dengue manifestations occur in up to 30% of cases, commonly spontaneous gingival bleeding, and can include palatal red or purplish spots, ulcers, lip crusts, and a metallic taste; distinguish from chronic gingivitis by abrupt bleeding with fever and body aches. Recovery of coagulation takes 1–2 weeks; resume invasive treatment 14–21 days after symptom end, with a complete blood count. In emergencies, use safe analgesics (paracetamol or dipyrone); avoid NSAIDs and aspirin. Interdisciplinary, conservative management prioritizes safety.

articleSummary: Measles (sarampo) risk rises in Brazil as Health Ministry warns of imminent reintroduction amid heavy World Cup travel, signaling high transmission risk in the Americas. In June a zero-dose of the measles-containing vaccine was advised for children 6–11 months to bolster protection in the most susceptible. Measles is highly contagious and airborne; a single case can transmit to about 90% of unimmunized contacts, with spread from six days before to four days after rash onset. Early signs include fever above 38.5°C, dry cough, conjunctivitis, and a facial rash that starts on the face and behind the ears before spreading. Complications comprise pneumonia (about 1 in 20 children), otitis media, encephalitis (1–4 per 1,000), and death (1–3 per 1,000). Diagnosis is clinical but laboratory confirmation is ideal; treatment is supportive. Vaccines available: MMR (triple viral) and MMRV (tetra viral); routine coverage targets 12 months through 59 years; pregnancy is a contraindication; during outbreaks, vaccination may be offered to infants 6 months–<1 year.

articleHeadline: Phase 3 trial of Ebola vaccine to begin within weeks in Congo
articleSummary: Phase 3 trial of Ebola vaccine Ervebo to begin in Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Ituri province to address the Bundibugyo ebolavirus outbreak. No approved vaccine exists for Bundibugyo; the outbreak has killed more than 2,000 people in the DRC as of Aug. 9 (CDC). The trial will use Ervebo, approved in 2019 for Orthoebolavirus zairense, with prior NEJM-lab results suggesting cross-protection against Bundibugyo. WHO designed the trial, to be implemented by a consortium including the DRC’s National Institute of Biomedical Research, CEPI, Institute of Tropical Medicine in Belgium, Doctors Without Borders, and Africa CDC. At a July 31 vaccine advisory board meeting, Ervebo was prioritized for inclusion; the trial could start about six weeks from that date (mid-September) but depends on DRC protocol approval, vaccine shipping to Ituri, and training. Long-term need for Bundibugyo-specific vaccines noted, with Oxford Vaccine Group and Moderna pursuing related trials.
